front: Requirement vs specification: what is the difference?
back: A requirement states what the business needs and why, without choosing a solution. A specification states how the solution meets it: fields, rules, screens, interfaces. The business approves requirements; the build team works from specifications.

front: Business, functional and non-functional requirements: one example each.
back: Business: stop overpaying duty on broker entries. Functional: the audit report flags lines whose applied rate differs from the expected rate. Non-functional: the report runs in under 5 minutes and keeps an audit trail.

front: What does MoSCoW stand for in prioritization?
back: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time). Won't-haves are agreed out of scope for now, which is what stops scope creep.

front: MoSCoW: how do you test whether a requirement is really a Must?
back: Ask: if it is missing on go-live day, can we still operate legally and safely, even with a workaround? If a workaround exists, it is a Should, not a Must.

front: What is an acceptance criterion?
back: A specific, testable pass/fail condition a requirement or story must meet before the business accepts it. Write it before the build starts so the tester and the developer read the same target.

front: What is the Given/When/Then pattern for acceptance criteria?
back: Given a starting context, When an action or event happens, Then an observable result follows. Example: Given a CN-origin item, When a 25% action takes effect, Then entries from the effective date use the new rate.

front: What is the user story format?
back: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit], plus acceptance criteria. Example: As a Research BSA, I want rates effective-dated, so that entries before a change keep the old rate.

front: As-is vs to-be process: what is each and which do you map first?
back: As-is is how the process runs today, workarounds and pain points included. To-be is the designed future process. Map the as-is first: it is the baseline for requirements, gaps and measuring the change.

front: What is a SIPOC?
back: A one-page, high-level process view: Suppliers, Inputs, Process (about 4 to 7 steps), Outputs, Customers. Use it to agree the scope and boundaries of a process before detailed mapping.

front: What do the letters in RACI mean?
back: Responsible: does the work. Accountable: the one person who signs off. Consulted: gives input before (two-way). Informed: told after (one-way). Each task has exactly one A.

front: Maker-checker: what may the maker never do?
back: Approve or release their own work. A second person checks it and records the review; the maker fixes the findings. Our team applies this to every standard cost update and released tariff model, also after day 90.

front: What is a Definition of Ready?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet before work starts: clear value, acceptance criteria, data sources known, dependencies identified, sized, and small enough to finish in one sprint.

front: What is a Definition of Done?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet to count as finished: built, tested against its acceptance criteria, reviewed (maker-checker), documented, and accepted by the business owner.

front: What is change control?
back: The process to request, assess (impact, risk, effort), approve, schedule and record every change to a system or agreed scope, so nothing reaches production without review and a record.

front: What is UAT (user acceptance testing)?
back: Business users confirm the system supports their real processes with realistic data before go-live. It answers 'can we run the business on it?', not 'does the code work?'.

front: UAT entry criteria: give four examples.
back: Build deployed to the UAT environment; system and integration testing passed with no open critical defects; test data loaded; test cases approved and testers available.

front: UAT exit criteria: give four examples.
back: All planned test cases executed; no open critical or high defects, or workarounds formally accepted; every requirement traced to a passed test; business sign-off documented.

front: What is regression testing?
back: Re-running existing tests after a change to confirm that what worked before still works. Needed for every tool change, patch or upgrade, not only for the feature that changed.

front: Defect severity vs priority?
back: Severity is the impact on the business or system. Priority is how soon it must be fixed. A wrong label on a management report can be low severity but high priority before a board meeting.

front: Positive test vs negative test?
back: A positive test uses valid input and expects success. A negative test uses invalid or edge input (blank HTS, end date before start date, duplicate line) and expects a controlled rejection or error message.

front: What is a requirements traceability matrix?
back: A table linking each requirement to its design, test cases and test results. It proves every requirement was built and tested, and shows what a proposed change will affect.

front: What is a parallel run?
back: Running the old and the new process or system side by side on the same inputs and comparing outputs before switching over. It costs effort but proves the new results tie out.

front: What is a data mapping specification?
back: A document mapping each target field to its source field or fields, with the transformation rule, data type, default, validation and owner. Conversion, interfaces and their tests are built from it.

front: What is a crosswalk (value mapping) table?
back: A table translating code values between systems, for example a legacy program code to the target system's USMCA code. Every source value must map to a target value or be explicitly rejected.

front: Data mapping: what is a transformation rule?
back: The logic applied between source and target: reformat, look up, default, concatenate, split or derive. Write it so developer and tester read it the same way, e.g. 'remove dots from the HTS; keep as 10-character text'.

front: What is a system of record?
back: The authoritative source for a data element; every other system reads from it or syncs to it. Ask it for each field you map, e.g. is item origin mastered in Oracle or in the trade system?

front: What is data cleansing before a migration?
back: Finding and fixing source problems (duplicates, missing values, invalid codes, contradictions) before conversion, each with a rule and an owner, so bad data does not move into the new system.

front: How do you prove a data conversion worked?
back: Reconcile source to target: record counts, control totals (such as the sum of standard cost), field-level checks on keys, and record-by-record samples. Explain and sign off every difference.

front: What is cutover?
back: The planned, time-boxed sequence that switches from the old system to the new: data freeze, final conversion, validation, go/no-go decision, go-live. It includes a tested rollback plan.

front: What is hypercare?
back: A defined period right after go-live with extra support: fast defect triage, daily checks of key outputs and quick fixes, before normal support takes over.

front: SQL: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?
back: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match. Use LEFT to keep, and count, orphans.

front: SQL: WHERE vs HAVING?
back: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test COUNT or SUM. Example: GROUP BY entry_no, line_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 finds duplicate keys.

front: SQL: in what logical order is a SELECT processed?
back: FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, TOP. That is why a column alias made in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE but can be used in ORDER BY.

front: SQL: the GROUP BY rule for the SELECT list?
back: Every selected column that is not inside an aggregate (SUM, COUNT...) must be in GROUP BY. You get one output row per distinct combination of the GROUP BY columns.

front: SQL: what does a comparison with NULL return?
back: UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, because NULL means the value is unknown. So column = NULL never matches. Test with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

front: SQL: why does WHERE program_claimed <> 'USMCA' skip lines with no program?
back: For a NULL program_claimed the comparison returns UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Write WHERE program_claimed IS NULL, or add OR program_claimed IS NULL.

front: SQL: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
back: COUNT(*) counts rows, NULLs and duplicates included. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. So COUNT(*) - COUNT(column) is the number of NULLs in that column.

front: SQL: what does COALESCE do?
back: Returns the first argument that is not NULL. COALESCE(LEFT(hts10, 2), 'UNK') labels lines with a missing HTS instead of letting them drop out of a report.

front: SQL: what is a CTE?
back: A common table expression: a temporary named result set defined with WITH and used in one statement. It turns a long query into named steps you can check one at a time.

front: SQL: what is a window function?
back: A function computed over a set of rows related to the current row, defined by OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). Unlike GROUP BY it keeps every row. Used for ranks, running totals, de-duplication.

front: SQL: how do you keep one row per key when a file was loaded twice?
back: Number the copies with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY the key columns ORDER BY ...) and keep the rows where the number is 1. Then check: clean rows = distinct keys.

front: SQL: you join entry lines to a rate table and the row count goes up. What happened?
back: Join fan-out: the rate table has more than one row per join key, for example two effective-dated periods. Add the missing key or date condition until the count equals the original.

front: SQL: how do you pick the rate in effect on the entry date?
back: Join on the keys AND entry_date BETWEEN effective_from AND effective_to. Then prove exactly one match per line: row count after the join equals row count before.

front: T-SQL: what does 12 / 9 return?
back: 1. Integer divided by integer truncates the fraction. To annualize 9 months write SUM(x) * 12 / 9, or use 12.0, never SUM(x) * (12 / 9).

front: SQL: why store money as DECIMAL, not FLOAT?
back: FLOAT is an approximate binary type, so sums can drift by fractions of a cent and fail to tie out. DECIMAL(p,s) stores exact decimal values.

front: SQL: why compute a rate as SUM(duty) / SUM(value) rather than AVG(duty / value)?
back: AVG of line ratios weights a $50 line the same as a $50,000 line. The ratio of sums weights by value, which is what an effective duty rate or PPV % means.

front: Data warehouse: fact table vs dimension table?
back: A fact table holds measurable events at a stated grain (entry lines, receipts) with numeric measures and keys. A dimension describes them (item, supplier, date, country) with attributes to filter and group by.

front: What is a star schema?
back: A fact table in the center joined by keys to dimension tables, with dimensions not chained to each other. Simple to query, and the shape Power BI models work best with.

front: What is the grain of a fact table?
back: What one row represents, e.g. one entry line. State it before building anything. Mixing grains, such as a header-level freight amount repeated on each line, double counts when summed.

front: Slowly changing dimension: Type 1 vs Type 2?
back: Type 1 overwrites the old value, so history is lost. Type 2 adds a new row with valid-from and valid-to dates, so old facts keep the value in effect then, such as an item's HTS before a reclassification.

front: Power Query vs DAX: which does what?
back: Power Query (M) imports and shapes data before it reaches the model: clean, merge, set types. DAX calculates on the loaded model: measures and calculated columns. Clean in Power Query, calculate in DAX.

front: Power BI: calculated column vs measure?
back: A calculated column is computed per row at refresh and stored: use it for attributes you slice by. A measure is computed when queried, in the current filter context: use it for totals and ratios.

front: Why must Effective Duty Rate be a DAX measure, not a calculated column?
back: The rate must be total duty divided by total value for whatever is filtered. A per-row rate column summed or averaged gives wrong totals. DIVIDE([Total Duty], [Total Entered Value]) recalculates in every context.

front: Power BI: what is filter context?
back: The set of filters in force when a measure is evaluated: slicers, the visual's rows and columns, page and report filters, spread through relationships. Same measure, different context, different value.

front: DAX: what does CALCULATE do?
back: Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context, adding, replacing or removing filters. Example: CALCULATE([PPV], Receipts[is_outlier] = FALSE()). It also turns row context into filter context.

front: DAX: DIVIDE vs the / operator?
back: DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, alternate) returns BLANK, or the alternate result, when the denominator is zero, instead of an error. Use it for every ratio, such as duty rate or PPV %.

front: Power BI: what relationship cardinality should a dimension-to-fact link have?
back: One-to-many: one item row to many entry lines, filtering in a single direction from dimension to fact. A many-to-many prompt usually means a duplicate key or wrong grain; fix the data first.

front: A Power BI total differs from your SQL total. What do you check first?
back: Filters (visual, page, report, slicers); relationships (inactive, wrong direction, unmatched keys); the measure definition (sum vs average, exclusions); and the refresh date of the data.

front: Power BI: a slicer shows '(Blank)'. What does it usually mean?
back: Some fact rows have a key with no match in the dimension, e.g. an entry line whose item is missing from the item table. Totals include them; fix the data rather than hide the blank.
